posts.title: Day four is when tracking dies

slides.text: Day four is when tracking dies.
Not day one. Day one is easy, day one is motivated.
Day two you log everything.
Day three you log most of it.
Day four you eat something awkward and skip it, and skipping once is the whole thing.
Logging a meal takes one photo, not a form.
The fix is not discipline. It is making day four take five seconds.

Make day four easy.

Log it rough. Just log it.

slides.text: Your week does not break on Wednesday.

Weekend eating is social, unmeasured, and someone else cooked it.
Two unlogged days is not two days of data. It is a week you cannot read.
One photo works on a restaurant plate too.
Log the weekend badly rather than not at all. That is the whole trick.

posts.title: The log of shame spiral

slides.text: The log of shame is why people quit.
It goes in a specific order, every time.
You eat something you did not plan.
You decide to log it later, which means never.
Now the day is incomplete, so the week is pointless, so you stop.
The log does not judge. It itemises and moves on.
Log the meal you do not want to log. That is the one that matters.
These are estimates you approve, not verdicts handed to you.
A log, not a verdict.

posts.caption: Nobody quits because the food was bad. They quit because one unlogged meal made the day incomplete, and an incomplete day makes the week feel pointless. The meal you do not want to log is the exact one worth logging.

Food is the same, and it works the same way.

Read it, do not grade it. That is the difference that lasts.

Three: log half of it now rather than all of it never.
Every one of these is editable after the fact.
Badly logged is logged. Perfect is the enemy here.
The app shows its work and lets you change it. Consistency beats precision.
Log it imperfectly. Log it anyway.
